1.why: A grouped bar chart is the clearest way to compare the counts of a categorical variable (class) across another (split). Placing *before* and *after* side by side shows exactly what the de-duplication changed.
1.insight: Train keeps nearly all of its images, because train copies are always kept. **Validation and test shrink**, and **glioma collapses in both**: most glioma images in the original valid and test folders were copies of training scans. After cleaning, only a handful of glioma images are left for evaluation, while the other three classes lose far less.
1.impact: Yes. The model will now be judged on genuinely unseen scans, so the accuracy reported to clinicians is trustworthy, and the model trains on the largest possible set of unique scans. The negative side is that **glioma, one of the most aggressive tumor types, has very few test images**. Its test recall is therefore a noisy estimate: one error changes it by several percentage points. A glioma score that looks good or bad on so few images should not be over-interpreted; validation results and the confusion matrices should be read alongside it.

2.why: A donut chart shows each class as a part of the whole, which makes the overall balance of the target variable easy to read at a glance.
2.insight: Pituitary and meningioma make up the largest shares of the cleaned data; glioma and no-tumor are smaller. The largest-to-smallest ratio is moderate (well under 3:1), so the data is imbalanced but not severely.
2.impact: Yes. It confirms that simple accuracy can be misleading and that **macro-averaged** precision, recall and F1 must be reported, so that the smaller classes count equally. It also shows that per-class weighting is enough and oversampling is not needed. The negative insight is that the smaller share of glioma and healthy scans means the model has fewer examples to learn them from, which increases the risk of misclassifying exactly these cases.

3.why: Bar and histogram views of resolution, aspect ratio and colour mode summarise the image *format* variables in one place. These properties decide the resizing and channel handling in pre-processing.
3.insight: **Every image is 640×640 (aspect ratio 1.0) and stored in RGB mode, and in all but 7 images the three channels are identical**, so the content is grayscale. The 7 colour images are web-sourced no-tumor scans with a faint tint or a coloured watermark. There is no variation in resolution or shape, which means Roboflow already standardised the images.
3.impact: Yes. Uniform input simplifies the pipeline: a single resize to 224×224 introduces no distortion, and keeping 3 identical channels lets the ImageNet-pretrained models be used without modifying their first layer. The limitation is that the original scanner resolutions are lost, so the model cannot use them as a feature. If real-world uploads arrive at other resolutions or with colour annotations, the app must convert them to the same format, or accuracy may drop. The deployment app will therefore apply the identical grayscale-to-RGB and resize steps.

4.why: All images have the same resolution, so the compressed file size is a cheap proxy for how much detail and texture an image contains. A histogram with KDE shows its spread, and the per-class KDE shows whether that spread depends on the class.
4.insight: File sizes vary widely despite the identical resolution, which shows that the amount of anatomical detail differs a lot between scans. The class curves overlap heavily but are shifted: images with more visible brain tissue compress to larger files.
4.impact: Yes. The wide spread means the model must handle a range of image qualities, which supports using augmentation. No image is so small that it looks empty or corrupted, so no quality filter was needed. The negative side is that class-dependent detail levels could become a shortcut: a model might partly learn 'how detailed is the scan' rather than 'what does the tumor look like'. Evaluating on de-duplicated, unseen scans guards against rewarding that shortcut.

5.why: For image data the most important univariate view is the images themselves. A grid of random samples shows what each class looks like and how varied it is.
5.insight: Each class contains **mixed MRI planes** (axial, coronal, sagittal) and **mixed sequences** (T1, T1-contrast, T2, FLAIR), and head sizes differ within the frame. Pituitary tumors appear near the skull base and midline, meningiomas are often at the brain's outer surface, and gliomas sit inside the brain tissue, often with irregular dark or bright areas. Healthy scans show symmetric anatomy.
5.impact: Yes. The variety in planes and sequences shows that the model must learn tumor appearance rather than one fixed view. This justifies flips, rotations and zoom augmentation and argues for pretrained backbones that already recognise generic shapes and textures. The negative insight is that plane and sequence are not evenly spread across classes. A model could learn 'sagittal view ⇒ pituitary' instead of the tumor itself. Such a shortcut would fail in hospitals whose imaging protocols differ, so the explainability section checks where the model actually looks.

6.why: A histogram with KDE and quartile lines is the standard way to study the shape, centre and spread of one numerical variable, here overall image brightness.
6.insight: Brightness is **right-skewed**. Most scans are dark overall, because a large part of each frame is black background, with a long tail of much brighter scans. The brightness range is several times wider than the typical value, so exposure differs greatly between scans.
6.impact: Yes. The wide brightness range shows that pixel values must be normalised (scaled to 0–1) and that mild brightness/contrast augmentation will help the model cope with different scanners. The negative side is that very bright or very dark outliers could be misread if the model relied on global brightness. This is examined per class in Chart 8 and tested formally in Hypothesis 1.

7.why: The foreground ratio measures how much of the 640×640 frame the head actually fills, capturing 'zoom' or framing. A histogram shows whether framing is consistent across the dataset.
7.insight: Framing is **very inconsistent**. Some scans fill most of the frame, while others show a small head surrounded by black background. The distribution is broad rather than peaked around a standard value.
7.impact: Yes. It tells us the model must be robust to scale, so random zoom and shift augmentation are included. Because the images are not cropped to the brain, part of the input is uninformative background. The negative insight is that if framing differs by class (tested in Hypothesis 2), the model could learn the framing habit of the source hospital instead of the pathology. That would make predictions unreliable on scans from new sites.

8.why: A box plot with the individual points overlaid compares the distribution (median, spread, outliers) of a numerical variable across categories. It is the standard bivariate view for numerical-vs-categorical data.
8.insight: Brightness clearly differs by class. **Glioma scans are the darkest**, meningioma is intermediate, and **no-tumor and pituitary scans are the brightest**. The boxes still overlap substantially, so brightness alone cannot separate the classes.
8.impact: Yes. It shows that global intensity carries some class information. This is why brightness augmentation is kept **mild (±10%)**: strong brightness changes could erase or distort a real signal. The negative side is that this difference probably reflects acquisition protocol and source dataset as much as pathology. A model that leans on brightness would be fragile across scanners, which is a risk flagged for deployment. Hypothesis 1 tests the difference statistically.

9.why: A violin plot shows the full distribution shape of contrast in each class (with quartile lines), revealing multi-modal patterns that a box plot would hide.
9.insight: No-tumor scans have the **highest and widest contrast**, glioma the lowest, and meningioma and pituitary sit in between. Some classes show more than one bump, which is consistent with a mix of MRI sequences inside a class.
9.impact: Yes. Contrast differences confirm that contrast augmentation should be **mild** and that per-image standardisation, which would erase contrast, is not used; only 0–1 scaling is applied. The multi-modal shapes show that the model must cope with several MRI sequences within each class. The negative side is that sequence mix, not biology, may drive part of the contrast difference, which is another potential shortcut for a model.

10.why: Global means (Chart 8) average everything together. A density plot of the individual *tissue* pixels, with background removed, shows *how* the gray levels inside the brain differ by class.
10.insight: All classes have most tissue pixels in the low-to-mid gray range. **Glioma is shifted towards darker tissue**, while no-tumor and pituitary have more mass in the brighter range. The shapes differ in their tails, which is where lesions (very dark or very bright regions) appear.
10.impact: Yes. Class differences exist at the pixel level inside the brain, not only in the background. That supports learning directly from pixels with a CNN instead of hand-crafted global features. The negative side is that the curves overlap strongly, so intensity alone cannot classify tumors. A simple threshold-based tool would give many wrong answers; learned spatial features are required.

11.why: A scatter plot with marginal distributions (joint plot) is the standard view for two numerical variables. Colouring by class adds the target to the picture.
11.insight: Brightness and foreground ratio are **strongly positively correlated**: the more of the frame the head fills, the brighter the image, because there is less black background. The classes form overlapping but shifted clouds. Glioma sits more in the low-foreground/low-brightness region, pituitary in the high-foreground region.
11.impact: Yes. Much of the brightness difference between classes (Chart 8) is explained by **framing**, not tissue, which is important for interpreting H1. That motivates zoom/shift augmentation, which weakens the framing cue. The negative insight is that framing is a property of how a hospital acquires and exports images. A model that learns it could fail on scans from other hospitals, which is a real deployment risk.

12.why: A heatmap of the class × split contingency table (counts plus column percentages) is the natural chart for two categorical variables. The chi-square test quantifies whether the splits share the same class mix.
12.insight: After de-duplication, **valid and test contain a much lower share of glioma than train**, because their glioma copies of training scans were removed. The chi-square test confirms whether the class mix differs significantly between splits.
12.impact: Yes. It shows exactly how much evidence each class has at evaluation time. Macro-averaged metrics weight every class equally, so glioma still counts fully in model selection even though it is rare in valid and test. The negative side is that overall accuracy on test is dominated by the other three classes, and a weak glioma model could look better than it is if only accuracy were reported. That is why macro-F1 and the per-class confusion matrix are the primary evaluation tools.

13.why: Averaging all images of a class reveals where the pixels of that class *systematically* differ from the rest. It is a pixel-location view of the class-vs-pixel relationship that no summary statistic can give.
13.insight: Mean images are blurry heads because the planes and positions vary, but the difference maps show consistent patterns. **Glioma** is darker overall. **Pituitary** and **no-tumor** are brighter, with a larger head footprint that extends further toward the frame edges, and pituitary shows extra brightness around the centre/skull-base region. The strongest differences lie at the **head outline**, meaning framing, rather than at specific lesion locations.
13.impact: Yes. It confirms that pooled location information is weak: tumors appear in different places. Models therefore need translation-robust convolutional features and global pooling, which is exactly what the chosen CNN architectures use. The negative insight is that the largest systematic differences are about head size and outline, not tumor tissue. This is the same framing shortcut seen in Charts 7 and 11, and it must be watched in the explainability maps.

14.why: A correlation heatmap summarises all pairwise relationships between the numerical image statistics in one view. Spearman correlation is used because several variables are skewed and the relations are monotonic rather than linear. `label_idx` is included only as a rough ordering reference.
14.insight: Brightness, contrast, foreground ratio, entropy and file size are **strongly inter-correlated**; they largely describe one underlying factor, 'how much tissue is in the frame'. Sharpness is related to file size (detail). No single statistic is strongly associated with the label code, since the class is not an ordered variable.
14.impact: Yes. The global statistics are redundant and weakly informative on their own. That supports letting a CNN learn features from raw pixels rather than feeding hand-crafted statistics to a classical model, and explains why this project uses deep learning. There is no negative-growth insight in itself, but the strong coupling of brightness with framing means any brightness-based cue is really a framing cue, which reinforces the robustness concern raised earlier.

15.why: A pair plot shows every pairwise scatter and every per-class distribution of the key image statistics at once. It is the most compact multivariate view of how the classes separate, or fail to separate, in this feature space.
15.insight: In every pair of statistics the four classes **overlap heavily**; no combination of two global statistics separates them cleanly. Glioma tends towards lower brightness, contrast and foreground, while pituitary and no-tumor tend towards higher values. These are trends, not boundaries. Tumor type is therefore encoded in *local spatial patterns* (shape, texture, location of lesions), which is exactly what convolutional networks learn, rather than in global image statistics.
